source.title: Deep Learning is Not So Mysterious or Different

record.tranche_reason: The paper presents a linear random-feature least-squares model with a model-size sweep and reports double descent, a conceptual test of double descent outside deep networks.
record.gate_note: Figure 1(f) ResNet results and Figures 1(d)-(e) noisy-label results are identified as adapted from prior work, so they are not recorded as this study's own results. The paper also cites other studies' results; those are not rows. Figure 1(g) is the study's own reported random-feature experiment.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a position paper. Its one own double-descent result is Figure 1(g): a linear random-feature least-squares model swept over feature count d. The text says the model shows double descent in test MSE once d passes n, which bears on V4 (double descent outside deep networks). The ResNet-18 (Fig 1f) and noisy-label (Fig 1d-e) panels are adapted from prior work and are not this study's results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue double descent (with benign overfitting and overparametrization) is not specific to neural networks or mysterious. They say it dates back to Opper et al. (1989) and reproduces in simple linear models. They argue PAC-Bayes and countable-hypothesis bounds and soft inductive biases explain it. They present effective dimensionality, which falls in the second descent, as intuition rather than as a predictive measure.
record.recipe_differences: The own reported result uses a linear random-feature least-squares model rather than a deep-network size sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: Effective dimensionality of the parameter covariance (inverse Hessian, α=10) decreases during the second descent in the linear random-feature model. The authors give a Marchenko-Pastur explanation: small Hessian eigenvalues grow as d exceeds n, which reduces variance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the interpolating regime, effective dimensionality of the trained solution decreases as parameter count grows, tracking the second descent in test error.

record.problems: For the own double-descent result, the text gives qualitative descriptions rather than numerical curve values, and reports no uncertainty or control comparison. The effective-dimensionality result is an association, not a test of predictive peak location.
record.rows_left_out: No own-result rows were left out. Adapted ResNet results in Figure 1(f) and adapted noisy-label results in Figures 1(d)-(e) were excluded because the paper attributes them to prior work.

untested.parts: No own deep-network size sweep; the ResNet-18 panel is adapted from Maddox et al. (2020).
No sample-size sweep near the interpolation threshold is reported for double descent. The Figure 5 polynomial sample sweeps are not described as showing a peak.
Only one non-deep model class (linear random features) is tested, with no systematic comparison across classes.
Prediction of peak location by an effective complexity measure, across any axis, is not tested.
No label-noise or regularization sweep for double descent; no multiple peaks examined.
Re-plotting against effective parameters to recover a U-shaped curve is discussed (citing Curth et al. 2023) but not done.

record.verdict_notes: Only Figure 1(g) is an own double-descent experiment (Appendix D: 'Similar to Maddox et al. (2020)'). Figures 1(a)-(c) and Figure 5 are own polynomial experiments on benign overfitting and data-size robustness, not double descent. Figure 5 includes an unregularized degree-15 polynomial over n=10-100, but the text reports no peak near n≈16, so it was not treated as a V3 result. The record's V5 'limits_scope' label was dropped, because tracking is not a test of predicting peak location.

versions.untested_parts: The study's own reported sweep is a linear random-feature model, not a deep network.
No sweep over training epochs or training time is reported as this study's own result.
No own result varies training sample size near an interpolation threshold to measure whether more data raises test error.
The own result is for one linear random-feature model, not a systematic comparison across model classes.

The study reports effective dimensionality alongside a model-size sweep, but does not test whether it predicts peak location, whether one measure works across size, epochs, and sample size, or whether it predicts peaks quantitatively.
No own double-descent experiment varies label noise or regularization to test peak causes, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimal regularization.
The study does not test whether re-counting complexity turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.check: Figure-only. The text states the linear model shows double descent in MSE as d grows past n, but gives no numbers, no uncertainty and no peak value. The setup is close to the random-feature models already shown in Belkin et al. (an original source), so this is a light replication.

rows.measure: effective dimensionality of the parameter covariance matrix (inverse Hessian)
rows.value: figure only; the text says effective dimensionality decreases as d increases past n
rows.note: This reports an association with the second descent on the size axis; it does not establish that effective dimensionality predicts the peak location.
rows.check: The text says only that effective dimensionality of the inverse-Hessian 'closely tracks the second descent', decreasing as d grows past n. It is computed at one fixed α=10 on the size axis only. That cannot show whether a single complexity measure predicts the peak's location along size, epochs or samples, as V5 claims. Relinked as cannot_determine and recorded under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: linear random-feature least-squares model with weakly informative features y+ε, feature count d swept past n
relationships.reason: The text states test MSE shows double descent with the second descent past d>n (r1). The result is figure-only, with no numbers or uncertainty.
relationships.display_finding: Test MSE showed double descent, decreasing again when the number of features d exceeded the sample size n.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: Effective dimensionality is reported to decrease alongside the second descent, but the result shows tracking rather than predictive peak location and covers only the size axis (r2).
